summary: Fryderyk Wiatrowski opens by asking the audience what tasks they would replace with a reliable autonomous browser agent, receiving suggestions like travel organization, expenses, and calendar management. He argues the current one-off prompting UI suits demos but not production. Drawing an analogy to hiring good employees, he emphasizes that effective agents should operate independently after initial training, generating tasks autonomously rather than requiring constant instruction. He distinguishes high-leverage activities (hiring) from low-leverage noise (scheduling), suggesting agents handle the latter. Their agent Jace demonstrates email-based meeting scheduling. Wiatrowski categorizes work into reactive modes (customer support, well-defined tasks) and proactive modes (founder roles, difficult to codify), predicting reactive jobs will be replaced first via trigger-based agent systems monitoring a meta-aggregator of Slack messages, emails, calls, and market signals. As foundation models improve and rule sets become more descriptive, proactive jobs can also be progressively replaced, moving toward AGI. Peter Albert then provides a comprehensive technical guide to building agents, outlining a complexity progression from prompting to cognitive architectures to fine-tuning to reinforcement learning, with each step adding capability but slowing iteration from hours to weeks or months. His prompting best practices include rewriting prompts with LLMs, using XML syntax, matching model fine-tuning distributions by preferring JSON/XML/markdown, minimizing per-token computation, using hierarchical classification, crafting specific chain-of-thought instructions, and reducing noise. For few-shot examples, he recommends focusing on the most important parts rather than showing full long examples and maintaining 10-20 examples to test prompts against. When prompting gains are exhausted, he advocates splitting tasks into multiple pieces with explicit state tracking, planning and replanning, verification steps, and scratch pads for intermediate work, while parallelizing to manage latency. For natural tool interfaces, he recommends key-value updates mimicking Python dictionary syntax, full rewrites over small diffs (since models struggle with diffs), avoiding recursive nested structures, and moving image reasoning into text form because text training data vastly exceeds image-language pairs. He notes the trade-off between component count and system brittleness. For fine-tuning, he recommends simulating real interactions with an LLM acting as a human, emphasizing prompt diversity and difficulty (citing Alpaca's too-easy prompts as a failure mode), distilling multi-step pipelines directly from input to output to reduce latency, and filtering data via rejection sampling or language model judges to achieve GPT-4-level performance on specific tasks. He positions reinforcement learning as a final step for optimizing multi-step agent systems using execution feedback or model judges, noting high setup costs and difficulty switching models.

sections.title: Introduction and Vision for Autonomous Agents
sections.summary: Fryderyk Wiatrowski introduces himself and Peter Albert as Zeta Labs co-founders. He asks the audience what tasks they would replace with a reliable autonomous browser agent, receiving suggestions like travel organization, expenses, and calendar management. He argues that effective agents, like good employees, should operate independently after initial onboarding rather than requiring constant prompting.

sections.title: Embedding Agents in Workflows: High-Leverage vs Noise
sections.summary: Wiatrowski distinguishes high-leverage activities (hiring) from low-leverage noise (scheduling meetings) and proposes agents handle the latter. He demonstrates their agent Jace, which can be CC'd into emails to automatically set up meetings based on calendar availability, showing a simple integration that requires no browser interaction.

sections.title: Reactive vs Proactive Jobs and Trigger Aggregation
sections.summary: Wiatrowski categorizes work into reactive (customer support, well-defined) and proactive (founder roles, hard to codify) modes. He predicts reactive jobs will be replaced first via trigger-based systems where agents monitor a meta-aggregator of triggers (Slack, emails, calls, market signals), perform upfront browser work, and seek approval. As models improve and rule sets become more descriptive, proactive jobs can also be progressively replaced.

sections.title: Peter Albert: Prompting Best Practices
sections.summary: Peter Albert outlines a complexity progression for agent building: prompting to cognitive architectures to fine-tuning to reinforcement learning, with each step slowing iteration from hours to weeks. He details prompting best practices: rewriting prompts with LLMs, using XML syntax, matching fine-tuning distributions (preferring JSON/XML/markdown), minimizing per-token computation, using hierarchical classification, crafting specific chain-of-thought instructions, and reducing noise by including only relevant context.

sections.title: Advanced Techniques: Few-Shot Examples, Cognitive Architectures, and Tool Interfaces
sections.summary: Albert advises focusing few-shot examples on key parts rather than full long inputs and maintaining 10-20 examples to test prompts. When prompting gains are exhausted, he recommends splitting tasks into multiple pieces with explicit state tracking, planning and replanning, verification steps, and scratch pads for intermediate work. For natural tool interfaces, he advocates key-value updates mimicking Python dictionary syntax, full rewrites over small diffs (models struggle with diffs), avoiding recursive nested structures, and converting image reasoning to text first since text training data vastly exceeds image-language pairs. He notes the trade-off between adding components (more brittleness) and reducing cognitive load per step.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Data Collection, and Reinforcement Learning
sections.summary: Albert covers fine-tuning data collection by simulating real interactions with an LLM acting as a human, emphasizing prompt diversity and difficulty (citing Alpaca's too-easy prompts as a failure mode). He describes distilling multi-step pipelines directly from input to output to reduce latency at some performance cost, and filtering data via rejection sampling or language model judges to achieve GPT-4-level performance on specific tasks. He positions reinforcement learning as a final optimization step for multi-step agent systems using execution feedback or model judges, noting high setup costs and difficulty switching between models.
